stance_basis: letter explicitly states the draft EIS is 'generally inadequate' and lists multiple deficiencies requiring correction
summary: The U.S. Department of Interior reviewed the draft EIS and found it generally inadequate in its discussion of the existing natural environment and related impacts. The agency raised multiple specific concerns including insufficient treatment of open/agricultural lands as wildlife habitat, lack of aesthetic impact discussion, failure to address flora and fauna species, and an objectionable concluding statement about resource commitment. The agency's comments were responded to point-by-point by the project preparers, who partially addressed some concerns while defending others.
complaint_summary: The U.S. Department of Interior found the draft EIS generally inadequate, raising concerns about: insufficient description of open/agricultural lands as wildlife habitat, lack of consultation with the State Historic Preservation Officer, missing flora and fauna baseline data, failure to evaluate aesthetic impacts, inadequate discussion of impacts on non-endangered plant and animal species, need for DNR involvement in landscaping, and an objectionable final paragraph minimizing resource commitment.

statement.text:
We have reviewed the above statement in our areas of jurisdiction and expertise and find that it is generally inadequate in its discussion of the existing natural environment and related impacts. To clarify these points the final statement should respond to the following comments.
General Comments
Throughout the statement there are repeated references to "unused open land" and to the inevitable transition of this land to commercial and residential use, "regardless of whether a freeway is built or not." We also note that under the land use inventory on page 79, 28 percent of the proposed corridor area is presently classified as unused open lands and 24.1 percent as agricultural lands. Both of these types have value as wildlife habitat and speculation concerning their eventual development does not eliminate the requirement for a description and quantification of their present natural environmental features. We suggest that such discussion be included in the final environmental impact statement (EIS).

I. The Proposed Highway and Surroundings
To assure that cultural resources will not be adversely impacted by the project, we recommend that the final statement show evidence of consultation with the State Historic Preservation Officer, who is Mr. James Morton Smith, Director, State Historical Society of Wisconsin, 816 State Street, Madison, Wisconsin 53706, and indicate any necessary steps which will be taken to comply with Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966 P.L. 89-665).
This section should contain a description of the flora and fauna species that utilize the project area in sufficient detail to establish pre-project conditions. This would in the a general description of existing fish and wildlife species (game and non-game populations) and vegetative cover. Particular attention should be given to urban wildlife populations and existing agricultural and open lands.
It is indicated on page 46 that 30.5 percent of the land area within the vicinity of the proposal is classified as unused open lands. The final statement should contain a more definitive description of these lands, including any immediate proposals for these areas and a general breakdown in relationship to land ownership patterns. We suggest that the areas labeled as "unused open lands" represent a significant and valuable resource in metropolitan areas as open space. Retention of such spaces is often given priority over commercial or other developmental uses, and "open space" should be recognized as a use in the final statement.
II. Alternatives
It is indicated on page 79 that the proposed project (alternative #5) would result in a higher percentage of loss in agricultural and open lands than any of the other alternatives discussed. Consideration of this loss should be thoroughly evaluated in the discussion of this alternative. Similar losses should also be discussed in the remaining alternatives.
III. Probable Impact Upon the Environment
This section fails to consider the impact of the project on the aesthetic values of the project area. We feel that the agricultural and open lands which will be utilized have inherent aesthetic values for open space, wildlife habitat, and natural areas. Converting these areas to that of a highway facility will adversely affect these values and should be discussed in the final statement.

On page 82, last paragraph, it is indicated that no rare or endangered species of plant or animal life will be disrupted by the proposal, but fails to discuss the impact of the proposal on other plant and animal species. It should be noted that vegetation aids the aesthetics of an urban area and provides habitat for both urban and non-urban wildlife. In turn, wildlife in urban areas is easy to observe and represents enjoyment to specialized wildlife observers and the general public. Therefore, removal of vegetation from urban areas represents a loss of both aesthetic values and wildlife populations and should be indicated in the final statement.
V. Steps Taken to Minimize Impacts
Design Considerations: It is indicated on page 111, third paragraph, that all lands acquired by the proposed facility which are not needed for actual construction of the freeway will be landscaped. We suggest that the landscaping program be designed and carried out in consultation and cooperation with the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources.
VII. Commitment of Resources
We recommend that the last paragraph of this section be deleted because it tends to reflect an early philosophy toward natural resource management that is no longer reasonable. The commitment of resources for this particular project may be small (depending on the standard of comparison), but when viewed in total, highways utilize great quantities of our natural resources.
Sincerely,
Staff Assistant to the Secretary
Madonna F. McGrath
Madorie G. McGrath
